title: Acting and Reacting in Different Situations (3)

instruction.text: Drag the events into the most likely order, with the first event at the top.

atoms.text: Josephine incorrectly answers a question in front of the class.
The next time she thinks she has the answer, she doesn’t raise her hand.

instruction.text: Imagine you just witnessed this situation and responded to it in the way described. How might this affect Josephine?

feedback.finish: You influence not only your own emotions, but also have influence on the feelings of others. It’s important to think about how you can make others feel with your words and actions. This can help you build positive relationships with others.

atoms.a: You tell Josephine that she was brave to try and that everyone gets the wrong answer sometimes.
atoms.b: Josephine feels better and feels like she can continue answering questions.

atoms.a: You don’t say anything to Josephine and are just glad you weren’t the one who got it wrong.
atoms.b: Josephine continues to feel bad and answers questions in class less and less.

instruction.text: Drag the events into the most likely order, with the first event at the top.

atoms.text: Rihanna, your best friend, is told she can’t play football with the boys at break time.
Rihanna feels excluded and unfairly treated.
As a result, she is in a bad mood when the next class starts.

instruction.text: There are several things you could say to Rihanna after she is told she can’t play. Imagine you respond in the way described. How might Rihanna react?

feedback.finish: Listening and being there for your friends is one of the best ways you can support them. This can help you build long-lasting friendships.

atoms.a: You ask Rihanna why she even wants to play football because you think it’s boring.
atoms.b: She feels even more upset because it doesn’t feel like you understand her.

atoms.a: You talk to Rihanna and tell her that you will go with her tomorrow when she asks to play again.
atoms.b: She has the courage ask again tomorrow.

instruction.text: Drag the events into the most likely order, with the first event at the top.

atoms.text: Arlo missed the bus this morning and got in trouble with his mum.
He was then late to class and realised he didn’t have his homework with him. His teacher was upset with him.
Arlo got very angry when Mr Lorning got cross with him. He talked back and got in more trouble.
After getting angry, he left the room and started crying.

instruction.text: There are several things that could happen after these events. Imagine Mr Lorning responds in the way described. How might Arlo react?

feedback.finish: Listening and trying to understand others is often a good way to make people feel better and to resolve difficult situations.

atoms.a: Mr Lorning listens to Arlo talk about why he was so upset that morning. He realises how hard Arlo’s day has already been and tells Arlo he can bring his homework tomorrow.
atoms.b: Arlo begins to feel better and isn’t so angry and upset for the rest of the day.

atoms.a: Mr Lorning sends Arlo to the headteacher, and Arlo misses even more of the lesson.
atoms.b: Arlo feels terrible for days, and his parents get even more upset with him.

instruction.text: Drag the events into the most likely order, with the first event at the top.

atoms.text: Michelle just went to the toilet.
When she comes back to the classroom, you notice that she forgot to zip her trousers back up.

instruction.text: Imagine you respond in the way described. How might Michelle react?

feedback.finish: It might feel awkward to tell the person directly, but it is always nicer than talking about them behind their back.

atoms.a: You tell Michelle nicely that her trousers are unzipped.
atoms.b: Michelle feels a little embarrassed, but quickly zips her trousers up. You both giggle and forget about it.

atoms.a: You whisper to your friend that Michelle’s trousers are unzipped, and you both giggle.
atoms.b: Michelle finds out and feels humiliated.
